claim: Participants traded episodic and incremental influences off rationally, depending more on episodic information when incremental summaries were more uncertain.
source: Across two large, independent samples of young adults, participants traded these influences off rationally, depending more on episodic information when incremental summaries were more uncertain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from two independent samples showing the relationship between uncertainty and episodic memory use.

claim: Incremental learning provides a simple mechanism for evaluating actions without maintaining memory traces of each individual experience.
source: This sort of incremental learning provides a simple mechanism for evaluating actions without maintaining memory traces of each individual experience along the way and has rich links to conditioning behavior and putative neural mechanisms for error-driven learning (Schultz et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on neural mechanisms and is based on established knowledge about incremental learning systems.

claim: Decisions may be guided by the retrieval of individual events, a process often assumed to be supported by episodic memory.
source: However, recent findings indicate that decisions may also be guided by the retrieval of individual events, a process often assumed to be supported by episodic memory (Bakkour et al., 2019; Plonsky et al., 2015; Mason et al., 2020; Bornstein et al., 2017; Collins and Frank, 2012; Bornstein and Norman, 2017; Duncan et al., 2019; Duncan and Shohamy, 2016; Lee et al., 2015; Wimmer and Büchel, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent empirical findings.

claim: The use of episodes has been detected empirically even in decision tasks that are well-trained and can be solved normatively using incremental learning alone.
source: Although theoretical work has suggested a role for episodic memory in initial task acquisition, when experience is sparse (Gershman and Daw, 2017; Lengyel and Dayan, 2007), the use of episodes may be much more pervasive as its influence has been detected empirically even in decision tasks that are well-trained and can be solved normatively using incremental learning alone (Plonsky et al., 2015; Bornstein et al., 2017; Bornstein and Norman, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies demonstrating episodic memory use in well-trained tasks.

claim: The brain judiciously adopts different decision strategies in circumstances for which they are most suited.
source: An overarching hypothesis is that the brain judiciously adopts different decision strategies in circumstances for which they are most suited; for example, by determining which system is likely to produce the most rewarding choices at the least cost.
evidence: This is a hypothesis statement based on theoretical reasoning about optimal decision-making.

claim: Uncertainty plays a key role in achieving a balance between deliberative versus habitual decisions that maximizes reward.
source: This general idea has been invoked to explain how the brain arbitrates between deliberative versus habitual decisions and previous work has suggested a key role for uncertainty in achieving a balance that maximizes reward (Daw et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on uncertainty and decision-making.

claim: Imbalances in arbitration have been implicated in dysfunction such as compulsion, addiction, and rumination.
source: Moreover, imbalances in arbitration have been implicated in dysfunction such as compulsion (Gillan et al., 2011; Voon et al., 2015), addiction (Ersche et al., 2016; Everitt and Robbins, 2005), and rumination (Hunter et al., 2022; Dayan and Huys, 2008; Huys et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on clinical dysfunction.

claim: When reward associated with an action is more volatile, people adapt by increasing their incremental learning rates.
source: Studies of this sort typically manipulate the volatility, or frequency of change, of the environment, as a way of affecting uncertainty about incrementally learned quantities. In line with predictions made by statistical learning models, these experiments demonstrate that when the reward associated with an action is more volatile, people adapt by increasing their incremental learning rates (Behrens et al., 2007; Mathys et al., 2011; O'Reilly, 2013; Nassar et al., 2012; Nassar et al., 2010; Browning et al., 2015; Piray and Daw, 2020; Kakade and Dayan, 2002; Yu and Dayan, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies demonstrating this effect.

claim: The benefits of incremental learning are most pronounced when incremental estimation can leverage many experiences or when volatility is low.
source: We, therefore, reasoned that the benefits of incremental learning are most pronounced when incremental estimation can leverage many experiences or, in other words, when volatility is low.
evidence: This is an inference based on the logic of how incremental learning operates under different volatility conditions.

claim: When the environment is either changing frequently or has recently changed, estimating reward episodically by retrieving a single, well-matched experience should be relatively more favorable.
source: By contrast, when the environment is either changing frequently or has recently changed, estimating reward episodically by retrieving a single, well-matched experience should be relatively more favorable.
evidence: This is a prediction based on logical inference about when episodic memory would be advantageous.

claim: 254 participants survived after applying exclusion criteria in the main sample.
source: A total of 254 participants survived after applying these criteria, with 120 participants failing to respond to the volatility manipulation (criteria iii) and 44 participants responding to too few trials (criteria i) or too quickly (criteria ii).
evidence: This is a direct report of the data from the study's participant sample.

claim: The RB combined choice model that included a separate hazard rate for each environment (RB2H) outperformed both RW models, the RB model with a single hazard rate, as well as other alternative learning models.
source: Participants were sensitive to the volatility manipulation and also incorporated uncertainty into updating their beliefs about deck value. This is indicated by the fact that the RB combined choice model that included a separate hazard rate for each environment (RB2H) outperformed both RW models, the RB model with a single hazard rate, as well as other alternative learning models (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Episodic value was relied on more when beliefs about incremental value were uncertain.
source: This is consistent with the hypothesis that episodic value was relied on more when beliefs about incremental value were uncertain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supporting the main hypothesis.

claim: The inclusion of RU at encoding time did not provide a better fit to subjects' choices than the combined choice model with only increased sensitivity due to RU at retrieval time.
source: and the inclusion of this parameter did not provide a better fit to subjects' choices than the combined choice model with only increased sensitivity due to RU at retrieval time (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: This result provides further evidence for a tradeoff between episodic memory and incremental learning.
source: This result provides further evidence for a tradeoff between episodic memory and incremental learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relationship between episodic and incremental sensitivity.

claim: Uncertainty about value provided by either memory system arbitrates the balance between them.
source: It also provides preliminary support for a broader version of our hypothesis, which is that uncertainty about value provided by either memory system arbitrates the balance between them.
evidence: This is a broader hypothesis supported by the pattern of results.

claim: All effects of environment and RU on episodic-based choice and subsequent memory were replicated in an independent sample.
source: We repeated the tasks described above in an independent online sample of healthy young adults (n = 223) to test the replicability and robustness of our findings. We replicated all effects of environment and RU on episodic-based choice and subsequent memory (see Appendix 1 and figure supplements for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by replication data from an independent sample.

claim: Participants relied more on episodic information when incremental summaries were less reliable, that is, more uncertain and based on fewer experiences.
source: We used a task that directly contrasts episodic and incremental influences on decisions and found that participants traded these influences off rationally, relying more on episodic information when incremental summaries were less reliable, that is, more uncertain and based on fewer experiences.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by experimental data.

claim: More uncertain episodic-derived estimates may reduce reliance on episodic value.
source: We also found evidence for a complementary modulation of this episodic-incremental balance by episodic memory quality, suggesting that more uncertain episodic-derived estimates may reduce reliance on episodic value.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the relationship between episodic memory quality and reliance on episodic value.

claim: The brain optimizes the balance between different forms of learning according to volatility in the environment.
source: Together, these results indicate that reward uncertainty modulates the use of episodic memory in decisions, suggesting that the brain optimizes the balance between different forms of learning according to volatility in the environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Decision-making can greatly benefit from episodic memory for individual estimates when available data are sparse.
source: Our findings add empirical data to previous theoretical and computational work, which has suggested that decision-making can greatly benefit from episodic memory for individual estimates when available data are sparse.
evidence: This claim references theoretical work and is supported by the current empirical findings.

claim: Sparse data arises early in learning a new task, but also in task transfer, high-dimensional or non-Markovian environments, and during conditions of rapid change.
source: This most obviously arises early in learning a new task, but also in task transfer, high-dimensional or non-Markovian environments, and (as demonstrated in this work) during conditions of rapid change (Lengyel and Dayan, 2007; Blundell, 2016; Santoro et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work and the current study.

claim: Control over decision-making by model-free and model-based systems has been found to shift in accordance with the accuracy of their respective predictions.
source: Control over decision-making by model-free and model-based systems has been found to shift in accordance with the accuracy of their respective predictions (Lee et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Humans adjust their reliance on model-free or model-based systems in response to external conditions that provide a relative advantage to one over the other.
source: and humans adjust their reliance on either system in response to external conditions that provide a relative advantage to one over the other (Simon and Daw, 2011; Kool et al., 2016; Otto et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Tracking uncertainty provides useful information about when inaccuracy is expected and helps to maximize utility by deploying whichever system is best at a given time.
source: Tracking uncertainty provides useful information about when inaccuracy is expected and helps to maximize utility by deploying whichever system is best at a given time.
evidence: This is a general principle about uncertainty-based arbitration based on established knowledge.

claim: Human memory is resource limited and prone to distortion and forgetting.
source: This may be especially important given that human memory is resource limited and prone to distortion (Schacter et al., 2011) and forgetting (Ebbinghaus, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established work on memory limitations.

claim: An observer equipped with perfect episodic memory would always benefit from using it to make decisions in the task.
source: Notably, in our task, an observer equipped with perfect episodic memory would always benefit from using it to make decisions.
evidence: This is a logical inference about optimal behavior in the task design.

claim: Participants vary in their episodic memory abilities, and this memory capacity is related to the extent to which episodic memory is used to guide decisions.
source: Yet, as our findings show, participants vary in their episodic memory abilities, and this memory capacity is related to the extent to which episodic memory is used to guide decisions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings on individual differences.

claim: Behavioral signatures of model-based learning might arise from episodic control via covert retrieval of individual episodes.
source: it is possible that behavioral signatures of model-based learning might instead arise from episodic control via covert retrieval of individual episodes (Gershman and Daw, 2017; Hassabis and Maguire, 2009; Schacter et al., 2012; Vikbladh et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Working memory plays a role in maintaining representations of individual trials for choice.
source: A related line of work has emphasized a similar role for working memory in maintaining representations of individual trials for choice (Collins and Frank, 2012; Yoo and Collins, 2022; Collins, 2018; Collins and Frank, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on working memory.

claim: Working memory is unlikely to account for the effects shown in this study due to capacity constraints.
source: Given the capacity constraints of working memory, we think it unlikely that working memory can account for the effects shown here, which involve memory for dozens of trial-unique stimuli maintained over tens of trials.
evidence: This is an inference based on known working memory limitations and the task design.

claim: New episodes are more likely to be encoded under novel circumstances while prior experiences are more likely to be retrieved when conditions are familiar.
source: Recent studies found that new episodes are more likely to be encoded under novel circumstances while prior experiences are more likely to be retrieved when conditions are familiar (Duncan et al., 2019; Duncan and Shohamy, 2016; Duncan et al., 2012; Hasselmo, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Shifts between encoding and retrieval states of memory are thought to be modulated by one's focus on internal or external sources of information.
source: Shifts between these states of memory are thought to be modulated by one's focus on internal or external sources of information (Decker and Duncan, 2020; Tarder-Stoll et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Shifts between encoding and retrieval are signaled by prediction errors based in episodic memory.
source: and signaled by prediction errors based in episodic memory (Bein et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2015; Sinclair and Barense, 2018; Greve et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Unsigned prediction errors, which are a marker of surprise, improve later episodic memory.
source: Relatedly, unsigned prediction errors, which are a marker of surprise, improve later episodic memory (Rouhani et al., 2018; Rouhani and Niv, 2021; Antony et al., 2021; Ben-Yakov et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: States of familiarity and novelty can bias decisions toward the use of single past experiences or not.
source: Findings have even suggested that states of familiarity and novelty can bias decisions toward the use of single past experiences or not (Duncan et al., 2019; Duncan and Shohamy, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Subsequent memory was improved by the presence of uncertainty at encoding.
source: While subsequent memory was improved by the presence of uncertainty at encoding, as would be predicted by this work, there was little effect of uncertainty at encoding time on the extent to which decisions were guided by individual memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's findings on subsequent memory.

claim: There was little effect of uncertainty at encoding time on the extent to which decisions were guided by individual memories.
source: While subsequent memory was improved by the presence of uncertainty at encoding, as would be predicted by this work, there was little effect of uncertainty at encoding time on the extent to which decisions were guided by individual memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's findings.

claim: Uncertainty and novelty likely operate in concert but exert different effects over decision-making.
source: It, therefore, seems likely that uncertainty and novelty operate in concert but exert different effects over decision-making, an interpretation supported by recent evidence (Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by the current findings and a citation to recent work.

claim: Volatility is likely to impact the noradrenergic modulatory system, which has been found to signal unexpected changes throughout learning.
source: These findings suggest that volatility, as defined here, is likely to impact the noradrenergic modulatory system, which has been found to signal unexpected changes throughout learning (Nassar et al., 2012; Yu and Dayan, 2005; Yu and Dayan, 2002; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation based on citations to prior work on norepinephrine.

claim: Noradrenergic terminals densely innervate the hippocampus.
source: Noradrenergic terminals densely innervate the hippocampus (Schroeter et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to anatomical work.

claim: A role for NE in both explicit memory formation and retrieval has been posited.
source: and a role for NE in both explicit memory formation (Grella et al., 2019) and retrieval (Murchison et al., 2004) has been posited.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Memory formation is facilitated by ACh in the hippocampus, which may contribute to its role in separating and storing new experiences.
source: ACh is also important for learning and memory as memory formation is facilitated by ACh in the hippocampus, which may contribute to its role in separating and storing new experiences (Hasselmo, 2006; Decker and Duncan, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on acetylcholine.

claim: ACh is heavily involved in incremental learning and has been widely implicated in signaling expected uncertainty.
source: In addition to this role, ACh is heavily involved in incremental learning and has been widely implicated in signaling expected uncertainty (Yu and Dayan, 2002; Bland and Schaefer, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ACh may play an important part in managing the tradeoff between incremental learning and episodic memory.
source: ACh may therefore play an important part in managing the tradeoff between incremental learning and episodic memory.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known roles of ACh.

claim: Uncertainty arises from many parameters of the environment, such as stochasticity (trial-wise outcome variance).
source: Indeed, while in this work we investigated the impact of uncertainty on learning using a well-established manipulation of environmental volatility, in general (and even in this task) uncertainty also arises from many other parameters of the environment, such as stochasticity (trial-wise outcome variance) (Piray and Daw, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about sources of uncertainty supported by citation.

claim: Volatility manipulations are a reliable means to modulate uncertainty in incremental learning.
source: The decision to focus on volatility was based on a rich prior literature demonstrating that volatility manipulations are a reliable means to modulate uncertainty in incremental learning (Behrens et al., 2007; Mathys et al., 2011; O'Reilly, 2013; Nassar et al., 2012; Nassar et al., 2010; Browning et al., 2015; Piray and Daw, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Valence has been shown to impact both uncertainty estimation and subsequent memory.
source: Still other attributes of the learning environment, like valence, have been shown to impact both uncertainty estimation (Aylward et al., 2019; Pulcu and Browning, 2019) and subsequent memory (Rosenbaum et al., 2022; Kensinger, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Multiple memory systems (differentiated by numerous behavioral and neural signatures) are involved in the types of repeated vs. one-shot learning measured in this study.
source: While a scheme like this is possible, much prior work (Duncan et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2015; Poldrack et al., 2001; Packard and McGaugh, 1996; McDonald and White, 1994; Wimmer et al., 2014) indicates that multiple memory systems (differentiated by numerous other behavioral and neural signatures) are involved in the types of repeated vs. one-shot learning measured here.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on multiple memory systems.

claim: Individual objects and their associated value were better remembered from putatively episodic choices.
source: Further, our subsequent memory findings that individual objects and their associated value were better remembered from putatively episodic choices lend further support to the idea that episodic memory is used throughout the task.
evidence: This claim is supported by the subsequent memory findings.

claim: Artificial agents endowed with episodic memory are able to exploit its rich representation of past experience to make faster, more effective decisions.
source: Recent advances in computational neuroscience have, for example, demonstrated that artificial agents endowed with episodic memory are able to exploit its rich representation of past experience to make faster, more effective decisions (Lengyel and Dayan, 2007; Blundell, 2016; Santoro et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational work.

claim: Many individuals in both the main and replication samples failed to meet the baseline performance criterion of altering the incremental learning rate between the low- and high-volatility environments.
source: Finally, it is worth noting that many individuals, in both the main and replication samples, failed to meet our baseline performance criterion of altering the incremental learning rate between the low- and high-volatility environments (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a direct report of the exclusion data.

claim: The relatively subtle difference between environments may have contributed to some participants' volatility insensitivity.
source: Thus, the relatively subtle difference between environments may also have contributed to some participants' volatility insensitivity.
evidence: This is a speculation about why some participants failed to detect volatility differences.

claim: Uncertainty induced by volatile environments impacts whether incremental learning or episodic memory is recruited for decisions.
source: In conclusion, we have demonstrated that uncertainty induced by volatile environments impacts whether incremental learning or episodic memory is recruited for decisions.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion supported by the experimental data.

claim: Greater uncertainty increased the likelihood that single experiences were retrieved for decision-making.
source: Greater uncertainty increased the likelihood that single experiences were retrieved for decision-making.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Episodic memory aids decision-making when simpler sources of value are less accurate.
source: This effect suggests that episodic memory aids decision-making when simpler sources of value are less accurate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The results shed light on the exact circumstances under which episodic memory is used for decision-making.
source: By focusing on uncertainty, our results shed light on the exact circumstances under which episodic memory is used for decision-making.
evidence: This is a summary of the contribution of the work.

claim: Participants completed a total of 320 trials in the deck learning and card memory task.
source: Participants completed a total of 320 trials and were given a 30 s break every 80 trials.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Each card within a deck featured an image of a trial-unique object that could reappear once throughout the experiment after initially being chosen.
source: Second, in order to allow us to assess the use of episodic memory throughout the task, each card within a deck featured an image of a trial-unique object that could reappear once throughout the experiment after initially being chosen.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: If participants encountered a card a second time it would be worth the same amount as when it was first chosen, regardless of whether its deck color was currently lucky or not.
source: Participants were told that if they encountered a card a second time it would be worth the same amount as when it was first chosen, regardless of whether its deck color was currently lucky or not.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design and instructions.

claim: A total of 418 participants between the ages of 18–35 were recruited for the main sample through Amazon Mechanical Turk.
source: A total of 418 participants between the ages of 18–35 were recruited for our main sample through Amazon Mechanical Turk using the Cloud Research Approved Participants feature (Litman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct report of the recruitment procedure.

claim: 120 participants failed to respond to the volatility manipulation.
source: A total of 254 participants survived after applying these criteria, with 120 participants failing to respond to the volatility manipulation (criteria iii) and 44 participants responding to too few trials (criteria i) or too quickly (criteria ii).
evidence: This is a direct report of the exclusion data.

claim: 44 participants responded to too few trials or too quickly.
source: A total of 254 participants survived after applying these criteria, with 120 participants failing to respond to the volatility manipulation (criteria iii) and 44 participants responding to too few trials (criteria i) or too quickly (criteria ii).
evidence: This is a direct report of the exclusion data.

claim: 223 participants survived exclusion procedures in the replication sample.
source: A total of 401 participants were again recruited through Amazon Mechanical Turk, and 223 survived exclusion procedures carried out identically to those used for the main sample, with 124 participants failing to respond to the volatility manipulation (criteria iii) and 54 participants responding to too few trials (criteria i) or too quickly (criteria ii).
evidence: This is a direct report of the replication sample data.
